newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia opens power plant, worries over supply.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia opens power plant, worries over supply.

text.p: Malaysia on Thursday opened southeast Asia's largest private power station, but said the supply of electricity in the country must be improved.

"I hope the IPPs (independent power producers) will be able to guarantee us reliable and efficient supply of power at all times," Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said at the launch of Lumut power plant in northwestern Malaysia.
The Lumut plant, operated by Segari Energy Ventures Sdn Bhd, is capable of generating 1,303 megawatts (MW) of power.
Segari is 75 percent owned by Malakoff Bhd, 20 percent by national electricity firm Tenaga Nasional Bhd and five percent by the national pension scheme, the Employees Provident Fund.
Officials with the project said it was the biggest of its kind in southeast Asia and third biggest in the world.
Mahathir said demand for electricity in Malaysia was expanding at 12.8 percent a year, outstripping economic growth, which has averaged well over eight percent a year for nearly a decade.
He said the government had to license IPPs as Tenaga could not cope with demand. Five IPPs were operating in Malaysia with a total generating capacity of 4,112 MW, he said.

Altogether, 12 independents have been awarded licences. The biggest of them, Bakun Hydro-Electric Corp (BHEC), signed an agreement this week with its underwriters for an initial public offering on the local stock exchange.
BHEC will operate the 2,400-megawatt Bakun dam, now being built in a forest in the Borneo state of Sarawak.
Up to the turn of the century, Malaysia is expected to produce more electricity than it will consume.
Last year, total capacity was 10,110 megawatts with peak demand at 7,063 megawatts, a reserve margin of more than 3,000 megawatts, or 43 percent.
Next year, the surplus is projected at 834 megawatts. But in the year 2002 the country is projected to be in deficit by 2,948. That could be largely alleviated when Bakun starts operating in 2003.
The excess power has put a strain on the transmission system of Tenaga, which is obliged to buy the power produced by the IPPs.
Last year, a 12-hour blackout over peninsula Malaysia caused by a trip in the transmission system sparked calls for an end to Tenaga's monopoly on transmission.
A similar blackout in 1992 led to Tenaga's listing on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange and an end to its monopoly on power production.
Mahathir said Malaysian companies, including Tenaga, have done well in winning overseas contracts in places such as China, India, Cambodia and South Africa.
"We are not short of skill at all, this a positive sign," he said.
Mahathir said the industry should also work towards developing a big manufacturing base for electrical components in Malaysia "as this will be the next thing on our agenda".

"We should look at vital components such as gas turbines and generators, transformers, switchgears and high voltage cables," he said. "There are ready overseas markets for these if local demand is not there."
